knowledge_point.title: Computing a Reciprocal Ratio Using the Pythagorean Identity

question.:question/problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186110756-draft/plots/187198204046c1535ad840c118fb8ed11f681e9f6765d5ab7b9a1d39f6ea993e.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $y$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{14},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $sec⁡\theta .$
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186110756-draft/plots/f7a79078eb90810a2827f08860e0e83be370b7ef3407b886717a379c68664a92.png)

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta$ as follows:

$$
x=cos⁡\theta ,\,y=sin⁡\theta
$$

We're given that $y=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{14}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
sin⁡\theta =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{14}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $cos⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{14}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{14})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{27}{196}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{169}{196}} \\  & =\pm \frac{13}{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $cos⁡\theta$ is positive in the first quadrant. So, $cos⁡\theta =\frac{13}{14}.$

Knowing that $sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{cos⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{(\frac{13}{14})}=\frac{14}{13}.
$$

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta$ as follows:

$$
x=cos⁡\theta ,\,y=sin⁡\theta

We're given that $y=\frac{\sqrt{11}}{12}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{12})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{11}{144}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{133}{144}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{133}}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $cos⁡\theta$ is positive in the first quadrant. So, $cos⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{133}}{12}.$

$$

Finally, we rationalize the denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}sec⁡\theta  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{133}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{133}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{133}}{\sqrt{133}} \\  & =\frac{12\sqrt{133}}{133}\end{aligned}
$$
